results.key_finding: Brugada syndrome is diagnosed with a spontaneous type 1 pattern, or with a fever- or drug-induced type 1 pattern accompanied by arrhythmic syncope or a family history. All patients should avoid drugs that may induce ST elevation (brugadadrugs.org), avoid excessive alcohol and large meals, and treat fever promptly with antipyretics. An ICD should be considered in patients with a type 1 pattern and arrhythmic syncope (IIa); quinidine or epicardial substrate ablation is an option for electrical storm or recurrent shocks. A sodium-channel-blocker challenge adds nothing once a type 1 pattern has been recorded.
results.title: 2022 ESC Guidelines for the management of patients with ventricular arrhythmias and the prevention of sudden cardiac death (Zeppenfeld K et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997-4126)

action_criteria.label: 12-lead ECG (standard and high-lead positioning V1-V3) on arrival
action_criteria.rationale: The 12-lead ECG is the first test in every syncope (ESC 2018); recorded during fever, with high right precordial leads, it documents the type 1 Brugada pattern on which diagnosis and ICD decision rest (ESC 2022).

action_criteria.rationale: Orthostatic blood pressure on active standing is part of the initial evaluation of every transient loss of consciousness (ESC 2018 Class I); it tests orthostatic hypotension, the competing cause, before a cardiac cause is accepted.

action_criteria.label: Targeted laboratory studies: electrolytes (BMP); troponin and magnesium accepted
action_criteria.rationale: Electrolyte disturbance (hyperkalaemia, hypokalaemia) can also produce or aggravate a Brugada-type pattern and ventricular ectopy, and troponin addresses myocarditis during the febrile illness; labs are targeted, not routine (ESC 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Structurally normal heart: normal LV and RV size and function, no valve disease or effusion

action_criteria.rationale: Echocardiography excludes structural heart disease, myocarditis and RV cardiomyopathy as the substrate of the ventricular ectopy (ESC 2018); a Brugada diagnosis requires a structurally normal heart.

action_criteria.label: Inpatient telemetry (Holter accepted) while febrile, with a defibrillator available
action_criteria.rationale: Syncope with a pulseless interval, a type 1 Brugada pattern and family sudden death is high risk: immediate in-hospital ECG monitoring is Class I (ESC 2018) while the fever persists.

action_criteria.rationale: During a febrile viral illness with ventricular ectopy, cardiac MRI excludes myocarditis and subtle RV cardiomyopathy that can mimic a Brugada pattern (ESC 2022); it is recommended, not required, after a normal echocardiogram.

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.

clinical_pearls: Brugada syndrome is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young adults in Southeast Asia, where it is known as SUNDS (Sudden Unexplained Nocturnal Death Syndrome) or 'bangungot' in the Philippines, 'lai tai' in Thailand, and 'pokkuri' in Japan
Fever is a common trigger that unmasks concealed Brugada syndrome and can precipitate ventricular fibrillation; prompt antipyresis is part of management.

A normal afebrile ECG does not exclude Brugada syndrome; ECGs during fever and with high right precordial leads increase sensitivity, and a drug challenge is reserved for patients without a documented type 1 pattern.
Brief myoclonic jerks are common during syncope of any cause and are frequently misread as epileptic seizures.
SCN5A loss-of-function mutations are found in 20-25% of genotyped Brugada patients; the mutation has autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and expressivity
diagnostic_traps: A prior normal afebrile ECG creating false reassurance
Prior syncopal episodes attributed to vasovagal or orthostatic mechanism without recognizing the fever-exclusive pattern
Brief twitching during syncope being misinterpreted as seizure activity rather than convulsive syncope
Influenza infection being accepted as the 'cause' of syncope through dehydration/hypotension rather than recognizing fever as a channelopathy trigger
Lack of awareness of Brugada syndrome's high prevalence in Southeast Asian (especially Filipino) populations

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Jerome Bautista is a 38-year-old right-handed Filipino-American man who works as an ER nurse, presenting after being found unresponsive in the break room at work. He was on shift and had been feeling unwell with influenza-like symptoms since the previous evening — subjective fevers, myalgias, headache, and sore throat. He checked his temperature at home that morning (38.8°C) but came to work as the department was short-staffed. Approximately 3 hours into his shift, coworkers found him slumped in a chair in the break room, unresponsive. They initiated BLS protocol and moved him to the floor. A coworker who was monitoring him reports that he was pulseless for approximately 5-8 seconds before regaining a pulse spontaneously. He was unconscious for approximately 30 seconds total and then woke up, appearing confused for only a few seconds before becoming fully alert and asking 'What happened?' No tonic-clonic activity was witnessed, though one coworker thought she saw brief 'twitching' of his arms lasting a few seconds. There was no tongue biting, no urinary incontinence, and no post-ictal confusion beyond the initial few seconds. On detailed questioning, Mr. Bautista reports 3 prior syncopal episodes over the past 5 years, all occurring during febrile illnesses: (1) Age 33, during a severe urinary tract infection with high fever — found on the bathroom floor by his wife, who estimated he was unconscious for less than a minute. (2) Age 35, during community-acquired pneumonia — witnessed collapse during ambulation on the ward (he was an inpatient), spontaneous recovery, attributed to orthostatic hypotension. (3) Age 37, during COVID-19 infection — his wife found him unconscious in bed and describes a 'terrifying' episode where she could not feel his pulse for what she estimates was 10-15 seconds before he gasped and regained consciousness. He was taken to the ER and had a normal ECG and normal troponin; the event was attributed to vasovagal syncope. Between febrile episodes, he has been entirely asymptomatic with no syncope, palpitations, chest pain, or exercise intolerance. He has no history of seizures. He has no cardiac history and takes no medications. He is particularly anxious because his father died suddenly at age 42 in the Philippines — the family was told it was a 'heart attack in his sleep,' but no autopsy was performed and no prior cardiac evaluation had been done. His older brother in Manila experienced a similar syncopal episode during a fever 3 years ago but was never evaluated.
